stories.byline: Ben Solak, Seth Walder and Matt Bowen
stories.body:
Value is value, no matter where -- or how -- you find it. And that's what we'll aim to do each week in this space: finding betting value.

Ben Solak, Seth Walder and Matt Bowen bring different perspectives into how they approach sports betting. Solak leans on his expertise in player evaluation and the X's and O's to find edges, while Walder relies on statistical models to pick out plus-expected value bets, focusing mainly on defense. Bowen, a former NFL safety, predicts positive matchups and game winners from tape study and his understanding of the league.

From spreads and money lines to totals and defensive player props, a good price might be found anywhere. Results will be tracked throughout the season, with flat one-unit wagers for each listed bet. With that, let's dive into our best bets, favorite defensive props and the top game to bet in Week 1.

Note: Odds by DraftKings and subject to change.

Jump to:

Bowen's Game of the Week | Solak's plays | Walder's props

Bowen's Game of the Week

Cincinnati Bengals at Houston Texans (-2.5, 46.5)

1 p.m. ET on CBS, Reliant Stadium, Houston

This line has fluctuated but at -2.5, I am all-in. Would I feel the same at -3? I wouldn't love it, but I'd be willing to bet Houston at home in a bounce-back game after the Week 1 loss to Josh Allen and the Buffalo Bills. Let's get into what to look for on both sides of the ball, and we'll finish with some props bets to play.

When Houston has the ball: Houston spent the offseason working on its run game, trading for David Montgomery and adding to the offensive front. And we saw a dedicated effort to run the football in Week 1, as Montgomery had 20 carries, with Woody Marks chipping in with nine. Now, was it super efficient? No. Montgomery averaged just 3.0 YPC, and the Texans registered a run block win rate of 74% (17th in the league). But it's clear that Houston wants the run game to be a foundational element of its offense. This can boost the passing opportunities for quarterback C.J. Stroud, who will see a Bengals defense featuring a rebuilt front anchored by defensive tackle Dexter Lawrence II and an underrated secondary that can mix both zone and man looks. I would look for play-action concepts (which mirror the run game) to attack the Bengals' two-deep zone shells (in-breakers to Nico Collins, if he plays) while also scheming up some shot plays. I truly think Houston looks to control the tempo on offense in this one, but let's keep an eye on third downs because the Texans need to beat man coverage from the Bengals there.

When Cincinnati has the ball: I want to see this matchup against the Texans' defense. Though the Bengals looked flat in a Week 1 win over the Tampa Bay Buccaneers (Joe Burrow finished with 254 yards passing, and Ja'Marr Chase had two receptions for 12 yards), they create conflict because of scheme and talent. The Texans have been a zone-heavy defense under DeMeco Ryans, but they will mix in man coverage (based on game situations), which creates must-see TV when corners Derek Stingley Jr. and Kamari Lassiter match against Chase and Tee Higgins. Tight end Mike Gesicki (78 yards receiving in Week 1) could find room to operate against Houston's split-safety and single-high zone schemes to attack the voids there. But, my main question is will the Bengals' offensive line keep the pocket firm for Burrow and generate movement up front in the run game? The Bengals held a pass block win rate of 53.8% in Week 1 against the Bucs (13th in the league), while Chase Brown averaged only 3.5 YPC. It's a different matchup this week against Houston edge rushers Will Anderson Jr. and Danielle Hunter. Burrow will need to hit some explosive play throws to win this one.

Leans: Texans -2.5 (-118), Texans moneyline (-142), Over 46.5 (-105)

Now, let's get to some prop bets ...

Ja'Marr Chase receptions OVER 6.5 (-109)

I expect a dedicated effort to get Chase the ball after he caught only two of four targets in the Week 1 win over the Bucs -- screens, unders and quicks that cater to Chase's explosive catch-and-run ability. Look for Chase to be involved early in this game plan.

Mike Gesicki anytime TD (+280)

Gesicki caught a Week 1 touchdown on a schemed throw to beat man coverage. Plus, the Bengals can set up Gesicki on zone beaters in the high red zone (seams, corners) to counter the Houston defensive tendencies.

Solak's plays

Green Bay Packers -3.5 (-112) at New York Jets

I'm grabbing a quick buy-low spot on the Packers, who were much better Sunday than the box score would indicate. The Minnesota Vikings scored 14 late points on defensive takeaways deep in Green Bay territory in their 39-22 victory. But the Packers had a better success rate (38.8%) than the Vikings (34.5%) and struggled only in situational spots. They were 3-for-12 on third down. On four red zone trips, they scored only one touchdown and one field goal. Those are the little execution problems that hurt a box score.

Going from facing a Brian Flores-coached Vikings defense to the Jets should make things far easier. Matt LaFleur has experience facing Aaron Glenn from when Glenn was the defensive coordinator of the Detroit Lions and generally has found success (46% offensive success rate, 0.04 EPA per play, 2.2 points per drive).

I thought about taking the Packers' team total, currently priced at 23.5 and juiced -135 to the over. I think the Jets' offense will be a functional group this season, but they need to run the ball and play clock control to win games against superior opponents -- and that might limit the Packers' total drives. As such, I'll go instead for the full-game spread at -3.5. I would play this no further than -120.

Tennessee Titans team total UNDER 15.5 (-105)

The Titans' offensive operation was the worst I saw in Week 1: play designs that were dead in the water, offensive linemen uncertain of their assignments, easy drops and bad routes from receivers and poor accuracy and timing from Cam Ward at quarterback. It's tough to find anything to hang their hat on from a 23-10 loss to the Jets.

It's worth remarking that Brian Daboll's offenses have been poor in Week 1 -- six, six and and zero points in the three seasons previous -- and then stronger in Week 2. But against this Philadelphia Eagles defense, it's tough to have much faith. Philadelphia's defensive front looked as deep and disruptive as ever against an average Washington Commanders front, and the Titans are comfortably one of the eight worst lines in football. Though defensive back Cooper DeJean was banged up in the Week 1 game and sat out practice Wednesday, the Eagles' outside corner duo of Quinyon Mitchell and Riq Woolen still poses a huge problem for the Titans' ability to create explosive plays through the air.

The talent difference here feels simply insurmountable. The Titans will need defensive takeaways or big special teams outputs to get into scoring range. I don't see them getting enough. I would play this up to -115.

New England Patriots -5.5 (-105) vs. Pittsburgh Steelers

The past four defenses the Patriots have faced are as follows: Seattle Seahawks (Week 1), Seahawks (Super Bowl), Denver Broncos (AFC Championship Game), Houston Texans (AFC divisional round). Even their wild-card opponent had a near-elite defense (Los Angeles Chargers). We are finally at a point at which we can buy low on the Patriots against an imperfect defense.

The Pittsburgh Steelers' defense was hardly tested in Week 1 against the Cooper Rush-led Atlanta Falcons. Drake Maye and the Patriots' offense -- especially with TreVeyon Henderson returning from a right ankle injury -- represent a far stiffer test. Even though wide receiver A.J. Brown is on injured reserve because of an ankle injury, the Patriots have had a long week since last Wednesday to prepare for his absence. Their wide receiver room, featuring Romeo Doubs, DeMario Douglas and Mack Hollins, is plenty deep enough.

On the other side of the ball, Pittsburgh's offense was dreadful against a Falcons defense that was low in my power ratings to start the season. The Steelers' 31.4% success rate was the worst of all offenses in Week 1, and their 4.1 yards per play was fourth worst. There were some drops and procedural issues that made the performance look worse than it was, but it wasn't a good outing. I like the Patriots' corners and their ability to press Pittsburgh's receivers, forcing Aaron Rodgers into low-percentage prayers while the elite defensive tackle duo of Milton Williams and Christian Barmore generate TFLs and sacks.

This number has been rising throughout the week. I wouldn't play -5.5 at anything past -110.

Lamar Jackson rushing yards UNDER 39.5 (-112)

Jackson's rushing under was a common bet for us throughout last season, when it was clear that the Ravens' quarterback was not healthy. He is healthy this season, as 16-yard and 19-yard scrambles in Week 1 against the Indianapolis Colts indicate. Jackson ended the day with 40 rushing yards on seven carries (after losing three yards on three kneels).

New offensive coordinator Declan Doyle put Jackson under center more than Todd Monken and Greg Roman had previously. Under-center alignments limit the opportunity for designed QB run plays, like read-options. Jackson's lone designed carry against the Colts was a second-and-goal play from the 5-yard line. Though Jackson is still dangerous on a scramble, if he's only going to get designed carries in short-yardage or goal-line situations, his potential for high-yardage days will be capped.

I expect the New Orleans Saints and Brandon Staley's zone-heavy defense to keep much better eyes on Jackson in the scramble drill than the Colts' man-heavy approach afforded. I'll also be looking for an under on Jackson's longest rush when that line posts, but I'd take this number down to 37.5.

Walder's prop bets

Note: More defensive props will be added as odds become available

Defensive plays

Chicago Bears D/ST anytime touchdown (+750)

One medium good game from Carson Wentz should not make us forget about the fact that he is still Carson Wentz, a QB plenty prone to mistakes. Certainly my model hasn't, which is one reason why it likes Chicago's defense -- which is probably not a great unit overall -- or its special teams' chances to return a touchdown. The fact that the Bears have a prolific offense and are more likely to be in the lead in this game -- thus forcing the Minnesota Vikings to put the ball in Wentz's hands -- helps. I'd bet this down to +700.

Carolina Panthers D/ST anytime touchdown (+700)

As of this writing, we don't know who the Atlanta Falcons' quarterback will be Sunday. Guess what? They're all great options ... for the Panthers' defense. We're betting on a defensive or special teams score against:

A banged-up Cooper Rush or
A banged-up Tua Tagovailoa or
Michael Penix Jr., in his first start back after ACL surgery, or
Jack Strand

No matter what we think of the Panthers' defense, we should take this bet at +700. I would bet it down to +640.

Offensive plays

Aaron Rodgers pass attempts UNDER 35.5 (-124)

That the Pittsburgh Steelers were the No. 1 team in pass rate over expectation in Week 1, per NFL Next Gen Stats, was arguably more of an upset than the Los Angeles Chargers losing to the Arizona Cardinals. Will it continue? I'm willing to bet it won't, at least for this week. Mike McCarthy has had both pass-leaning and run-leaning teams in the past, but he also doesn't have a particularly good quarterback right now, so it hardly seems to make sense that they would keep up the pattern. That's why I'm agreeing with my pass attempts model, which thinks this line is too high for Rodgers, even heading into a game in which the Steelers are underdogs and will have to keep up with the New England Patriots' offense. I would bet this down to -150.

Rhamondre Stevenson receptions OVER 2.5 (-153)

The entire league ran zone coverage at a higher rate in Week 1 than in any season in our dataset (since 2017), but no team epitomized that more than the Steelers. Under coordinator Patrick Graham, the Steelers ran zone 89% of the time. Why does that matter for this bet? Since 2023, running backs have caught passes on man-coverage plays 8% of the time but 15% of the time against zone. That massive disparity plays into our hands here with Stevenson facing the Steelers. I opted for the conservative option at over 2.5, but I don't mind betting the longer-odds alts on this, either.

Malik Willis 24+ completions (+910)

I thought there was a chance the Miami Dolphins would go run-heavy to the extreme with their offense, but in Week 1 it was more of a normal split than I was expecting. Malik Willis threw 27 passes, and the Dolphins ranked 11th in pass rate over expected. My attempts model sees value in the extreme tail outcome here, and I don't think it's that hard to imagine. If the Dolphins fall way behind in this game -- and I suspect they will against the 49ers -- they'll be forced to pass and pass and pass. And there also might be plenty of short throws available for Willis to make. I like this long shot.

stories.headline: MLB playoffs 2026: Fatal October flaws for every contender
stories.summary: Tired of seeing your favorite team go home early in the postseason? Here's one thing each current playoff team needs to address to make a deep run.
stories.body:
With the 2026 Major League Baseball playoffs just around the corner, two quotes come to mind from Billy Beane, the former major league outfielder and current Athletics front office executive.

"How can you not be romantic about baseball?" Beane's character asks in the movie "Moneyball." Maybe he had this year's American League West race in mind.

The real Billy Beane, in a despondent moment in 2002, told Michael Lewis, author of the "Moneyball" book, "My s--- doesn't work in the playoffs."

Beane's Oakland teams never did reach a World Series, which was more about the high variance of short playoff series rather than his stuff not really working, but you can apply that quote to each of this year's playoff contenders. They all have fatal flaws.

(Of course, two of them will reach the World Series anyway ... and that's the romance part.)

Let's break down what each contender's fatal flaw is and whether it will sink them in October -- or whether they can overcome it to make a deep postseason run.

NATIONAL LEAGUE

Milwaukee Brewers

Fatal flaw: Lack of power (tied for 28th in the majors in home runs)

The Brewers have clinched their fourth consecutive NL Central title and eighth playoff appearance in nine seasons with what has been the best team in franchise history. Last year's squad set the franchise record with 97 wins, and this year's team should reach 100 with a well-rounded roster built around likely Cy Young winner Jacob Misiorowski.

How they got there is fascinating: Only the Cubs have scored more runs than Milwaukee, even though the Brewers might end up last in the majors in home runs. Only 32.6% of Milwaukee's runs have been scored via the long ball, easily the lowest percentage in the majors, where the overall average for 2026 is 40.6%. And here's the thing to worry about: Over the past 10 postseasons (leaving out 2020), the percentage of runs scored via the home run has gone up each year compared to the regular season.

This means hitting home runs is even more important in the postseason. Perfectly executed small ball can certainly play a role at times, but it's more difficult to put together sustained rallies against better pitching without mixing in some power. Over the past 10 postseasons, again excluding 2020, the playoff team with the fewest home runs in the regular season has gone 17-29 and failed to reach a World Series.

On the other hand, the team with the most home runs -- it has been the Yankees five times -- has reached only one World Series, with the Yankees losing to the Dodgers in 2024 (Los Angeles was third in home runs that season, just four behind New York). Those teams have gone 31-41, so they've played 72 postseason games compared to 46 for the teams at the bottom in home runs.

This doesn't mean you should write off the Brewers. For one thing, they have been hitting and slugging much better since June compared to the first two months:

April-May: .242/.328/.359, 0.71 home runs per game

June-September: .269/.349/.430, 1.10 home runs per game

Jackson Chourio sat out April, Jake Bauers has been terrific and Joey Ortiz has been one of the best hitters in the majors since the All-Star break, so the current lineup is deeper than the one early in the season. The Brewers usually find ways to score -- they've been held to one run or zero runs only 12 times all season, six fewer than any other team -- and if Misiorowski and Logan Henderson and the bullpen are dealing, they only have to hit more home runs than their opponents.

Los Angeles Dodgers

Fatal flaw: Second-half offensive struggles (tied for 16th in runs since July 1)

The Dodgers are accustomed to taking a loaded offense into the postseason: They were first in runs in 2020, fourth in 2021 (first in the pre-DH NL), first in 2022, second in 2023, second in 2024 and second in 2025. They still rank fourth in 2026, but the runs have been much harder to come by since early July.

Injuries have played a part: Shohei Ohtani's knee, Freddie Freeman's knee, Andy Pages' fractured left hand and Will Smith sat out all of July and August. But there is still some uncertainty with those injuries: Ohtani won't return until five games are left in the regular season, Freeman is playing through his sore knee and Pages has yet to return. The lineup is old -- only Pages and Kyle Tucker are younger than 30 years old among the regulars -- and might once again be counting on Miguel Rojas and Enrique Hernandez to come up big in the postseason. The Dodgers will need Ohtani to quickly find his groove -- or maybe even rookie Josue De Paula plays a role somewhere.

Minus Ohtani, who won't pitch again this season, the rotation is still strong with the big three of Yoshinobu Yamamoto, Tarik Skubal and Blake Snell, with Tyler Glasnow probably slotting in as the fourth starter. Caveat: Snell left his start Wednesday after one inning because of groin tightness, so keep an eye on that situation. The bullpen certainly has some issues with Edgardo Henriquez on the injured list and Edwin Diaz now looking as if he won't even be on the postseason roster. Blake Treinen might need to get some key outs again.

Bottom line: Even with Yamamoto and Skubal, this looks like the most flawed Dodgers team during this long run of postseason appearances.

Atlanta Braves

Fatal flaw: Can they hit in the postseason? (.186 average from 2022 to 2024)

After winning the World Series in 2021, the Braves had disappointing NLDS exits in 2022 and 2023, following 100-win regular seasons, and then a wild-card defeat in 2024 (before missing the playoffs last season). They went 2-8 in those three abbreviated postseason series, hitting just .186 while averaging 2.5 runs per game.

The 2026 team includes essentially the same group of players that struggled in those postseasons, plus second-year catcher/DH Drake Baldwin. The Braves do some things well on offense, including hitting home runs: Matt Olson has 39, and Baldwin, Michael Harris II and Ozzie Albies have each surpassed 20 home runs, with Ronald Acuña Jr. and Austin Riley closing in on 20. That's power up and down the lineup, even if Acuña and Riley have been much more dangerous players in the past.

The one thing the Braves don't do is draw many walks, as they rank 28th in walk rate and 29th in chase rate. They have several aggressive swingers in the likes of Harris, Albies, Mauricio Dubon and even Baldwin -- hitters that good pitchers can exploit in the postseason.

Chicago Cubs

Fatal flaw: The ninth inning (Jacob Webb leads club with nine saves)

It doesn't feel good heading into the postseason and wondering who is going to get the ball in the ninth inning. Webb is a journeyman right-hander with a below-average fastball pitching for his fourth team in four seasons. He became the closer in June but has now blown four consecutive save opportunities, losing three of those games.

Maybe Chicago goes with Ryan Zeferjahn? Acquired from the Los Angeles Angels at the trade deadline, he at least has a closer's fastball (averaging 97 mph) and has picked up the past two saves this month for the Cubs, but he walks too many batters and has a 4.09 ERA on the season (5.65 with Chicago). Ryan Rolison? The lefty picked up a save earlier in September against the Brewers, but right-handed batters have an OPS over .900 against him. Daniel Palencia? Last year's closer hasn't been trusted in high-leverage situations since returning from the IL.

It's a mess. The Dodgers managed to survive their closer issues last October, but they had starting pitching depth they could use in relief, which the Cubs don't have. The Rangers had a bad bullpen in 2023 that got hot at the right time, so it's possible. But Cubs manager Craig Counsell is going to go through a lot of antacids if his team makes a deep run.

Philadelphia Phillies

Fatal flaw: Jesus Luzardo's injury (out because of shoulder inflammation)

The Phillies don't have a great offense, they definitely don't play great defense and the bullpen has been shaky at times, so their path to World Series heroics runs through Cristopher Sanchez, Zack Wheeler and Luzardo. In fact, Luzardo mighthave been in line to start the first game of the playoffs the way he had been pitching, with a 1.08 ERA over his past seven starts and 1.70 since June 10.

The Phillies remain hopeful he can return for the playoffs, but they also haven't announced any timetable. They probably will have to survive at least the wild-card series without him, which pushes Aaron Nola into the third game if needed. That might work: Nola has been pitching his best baseball in a few years, with a 2.38 ERA over his past nine starts. That ERA is a little misleading, though, as he has still been a little homer-prone and has a 4.44 FIP in that span.

And if the Phillies advance and Luzardo still can't make it back, that puts rookie Andrew Painter in the four-man rotation. He has been better since returning from the minors so it's not a lost cause, but you can see why president of baseball operations Dave Dombrowski has been getting some heat for not adding a starter at the trade deadline.

Not to mention: With final-week series against the Brewers and Rays, the Phillies still have to get to the playoffs in the first place.

San Diego Padres

Fatal flaw: Rotation doesn't miss bats (29th in strikeout rate since Aug. 1)

We're going to the beginning of August to assess the rotation, since that includes Casey Mize and Robbie Ray, acquired at the trade deadline. The problem is Mize has been terrible with the Padres, with a 5.97 ERA and only 22 strikeouts and nine home runs in 37⅔ innings. The way he has been pitching, he doesn't even project as a viable option for the playoffs right now. Ray has been almost as bad, with a 5.35 ERA and 24 walks in 33⅔ innings. Michael King is the ace, but even he doesn't miss a ton of bats, ranking 75th out of 132 pitchers who have thrown at least 100 innings in strikeout rate.

San Diego has that great bullpen, of course, so it won't need its starters to pitch a lot of innings, and the offense has been excellent in the second half after an awful first half, so at least that concern has been alleviated. The Padres still need to get in -- the season-ending series against the Diamondbacks might determine the final wild card -- but they'll need something from their starters to make that long-awaited World Series run.

Arizona Diamondbacks

Fatal flaw: Rotation doesn't miss bats (21st since Aug. 1)

The Diamondbacks still have to get in, but if they do, they face the same problem as the Padres, with a rotation that doesn't offer the power pitching and swing-and-miss stuff that executives want in October.

Eduardo Rodriguez has had an amazing season despite a below-average K rate, but the batted ball metrics suggest he has been a little bit lucky and has relied on a high strand rate. Merrill Kelly and Brandon Pfaadt had some big moments in Arizona's 2023 World Series run, but they rank 124th and 120th, respectively, on that list of 132 pitchers in strikeout rate.

AMERICAN LEAGUE

Tampa Bay Rays

Fatal flaw: Lineup depth (24th in OPS from 7-8-9 slots in lineup)

There's no doubting the top part of the Tampa Bay lineup, with Yandy Diaz, Jonathan Aranda and Junior Caminero, plus trade acquisition Liam Hicks has moved into the cleanup spot against right-handed pitching. But the bottom third of the lineup has been an issue for most of the season. Is that a problem for the playoffs? It does feel as if recent World Series participants have had deep lineups and haven't had to rely on only a few stars. Let's check that hypothesis by seeing how the World Series teams ranked in OPS from their 7-8-9 hitters in the regular season (going back to 2022 when the NL instituted the DH):

2025 Dodgers: 17th

2025 Blue Jays: 9th

2024 Dodgers: 9th

2024 Yankees: 16th

2023 Rangers: 5th

2023 D-backs: 21st

2022 Astros: 24th

2022 Phillies: 5th

OK, maybe not a big indicator, but it's something. Now let's see how those 7-8-9 slots actually hit in the postseason:

2025 Dodgers: .218/.275/.311, 3 HR, 15 RBIs in 17 G

2025 Blue Jays: .251/.299/.362, 4 HR, 25 RBIs in 18 G

2024 Dodgers: .235/.303/.398, 8 HR, 21 RBIs in 16 G

2024 Yankees: .240/.355/.377, 4 HR, 17 RBIs in 14 G

2023 Rangers: .250/.335/.472, 9 HR, 22 RBIs in 17 G

2023 D-backs: .231/.297/.364, 6 HR, 17 RBIs in 17 G

2022 Astros: .164/.252/.224, 2 HR, 8 RBIs in 13 G

2022 Phillies: .180/.256/.286, 2 HR, 18 RBIs in 17 G

A stronger indicator here. Miguel Rojas, the No. 9 batter, kept the Dodgers' season alive last year with that tying home run in the ninth inning of Game 7. In 2024, Enrique Hernandez had a 1.069 OPS from the bottom of the order for L.A. while Max Muncy and Will Smith also hit there at times. The bottom of the order was absolutely huge for the Rangers in 2023. Only the Astros in 2022 won without getting much from the bottom third, but that was the postseason that Houston's pitching was nearly untouchable.

New York Yankees

Fatal flaw: Offensive strikeout rate (27th in the majors)

The Yankees are somehow ninth in the majors in runs despite not having Aaron Judge for 100 days and suffering through long stretches of offensive futility without him. Now they're battling more injuries, with Jazz Chisholm Jr. and Trent Grisham on the IL, and Judge, just back from the IL, leaving Wednesday's game because of leg tightness.

As always, the Yankees hit home runs -- only the Cubs have more. But it comes with a price: a lot of swing-and-miss. Can a team make a run to the World Series with a high strikeout rate? Going back to 2022 and the universal DH, no team in the bottom half of strikeout rate has reached the World Series:

2025 Dodgers: 12th

2025 Blue Jays: 1st

2024 Dodgers: 11th

2024 Yankees: 9th

2023 Rangers: 15th

2023 D-backs: 4th

2022 Astros: 2nd

2022 Phillies: 15th

After reaching the World Series in 2024, the Yankees have gone backward in the strikeout department, ranking 25th last season and even lower this year (a problem exacerbated by Spencer Jones and his 36% K rate, if he has to play center field over the injured Grisham).

Boston Red Sox

Fatal flaw: Middle infield (26th in OPS from 2B/SS)

It has been a revolving door at both middle infield positions all season as the Red Sox have started seven players at second base and six at shortstop, with Trevor Story's 55 games started at shortstop the most at either position. Not only has the combined offense from those spots been near the bottom of the league, but the Sox rank 19th in defensive runs saved at second base and 27th at shortstop.

Let's start with Story, since interim manager Chad Tracy seems committed to him as the shortstop. Since Story returned from the IL on Aug. 30, he has hit .349 in 16 games. It's a fluke: He has one home run, one walk, 18 strikeouts and a 49% chase rate. His average exit velocity of 82.5 mph ranks 180th out of 185 players since that date. A once dynamic fielder, his defensive metrics have been subpar for a couple of years now.

With Anthony Seigler on the IL because of wrist inflammation, Nick Sogard is the regular at second base now, although veteran Isiah Kiner-Falefa might start against lefties. Sogard has hit well, and his defense is fine (he has played all over the infield, even starting four games at shortstop). Andruw Monasterio filled in at shortstop for much of the summer and can hit lefties, but he has barely played since Story returned. Frankly, Monasterio and Kiner-Falefa are probably both better options than Story, but we'll see how Tracy plays this final week and into October.

Cleveland Guardians

Fatal flaw: Lack of power (tied for 28th in home runs)

Cleveland falls into the same boat as the Brewers, except the Guardians don't have Milwaukee's ability to hit for average or overall depth. They did add Jo Adell and Nathaniel Lowe at the trade deadline, and though that pair is not the only reason, the offense has been much better since then:

Through Aug. 3: .231/.310/.370, 3.95 runs per game (29th)

Since Aug. 3: .251/.324/.386, 4.63 runs per game (tied for eighth)

Steven Kwan's turnaround has really been the big key, as he has posted a .406 OBP since Aug. 4 and is tied for fourth in the majors in runs. If he keeps getting on base and Jose Ramirez gets hot -- unfortunately, he has been bad in the postseason in his career (.234/.316/.365) -- you never know in the wild and wacky and unremarkable AL.

Chicago White Sox

Fatal flaw: Bullpen is out of gas (see Cleveland series)

The White Sox are running on fumes. Manager Will Venable has tried to work around the team's lack of pitching depth by using openers and relying heavily on a bullpen that has pitched the most innings in the majors. But the overworked pen paid the toll in losing the final two games of the Cleveland series this week, allowing the Guardians to leap into first place in the division.

On Tuesday, Grant Taylor tried to finish a two-inning save but blew the game in the bottom of the ninth, his fourth straight nonscoreless appearance. The next day, Hagen Smith tried to pitch two innings for the fourth time in seven days but tired and walked two batters. Sean Newcomb came on and served up the deciding home run. It was the fifth time in six appearances he has given up at least one run after he finished August with two straight three-inning outings.

The offense is also running out of steam, hitting .207 in September with a ton of strikeouts -- they struck out 36 times in three games against Cleveland and are averaging over 10 strikeouts in September. It has been a fun ride, but the White Sox are precariously holding on to a playoff spot.

Houston Astros

Fatal flaw: Starting pitching ... ? (27th in rotation ERA)

The worst nightmare for fans outside of Houston: The Astros win the AL West with a sub-.500 record and then get hot and give us the first losing team to reach a World Series. Fun! Hey, in the AL, anything is possible -- and the Astros' bullpen has been pretty good of late with a dominant Josh Hader, and any lineup with Yordan Alvarez has the potential to do enough damage (although Alvarez will need to heat up again just to get Houston to the postseason). The Astros are third in the majors in home runs, so they do have power.

The starting pitching makes that scenario a little less plausible, although we should point out that the rotation has a 3.15 ERA in September (fourth in the majors) with Hunter Brown and Hayden Wesneski both pitching well. Even Cristian Javier has now had three good starts in a row. And Peter Lambert has been the one consistent and healthy starter throughout the season for the Astros. So let's see: dominant closer, the best hitter in the game this season, power and a rotation that has been mostly awful all season but is peaking at the right time. Consider yourself warned.

Texas Rangers

Fatal flaw: Struggles against right-handed pitching (26th in OPS)

The Rangers have managed to hang around all season, hovering around .500 without any big swings in momentum in either direction -- never more than three games out of first place -- and four straight wins heading into Thursday's series finale against the Red Sox moved them into a tie with the Astros atop the division. Nathan Eovaldi is back after sitting out more than a month and pitched the final four innings in relief Wednesday, giving up only one hit, so that will help the pitching staff.

The offense has been the biggest issue throughout the season, particularly against right-handers. Left-handed hitters Brandon Nimmo and Corey Seager have both fared better against southpaws (although Seager is hitting everyone in September). Team MVP Ezequiel Duran has a .406 OBP against lefties, .299 against righties. Jake Burger has a .908 OPS against left-handers, .666 against right-handers. Josh Jung is hitting .352 against lefties, .281 against righties.

This suggests the Rangers might match up better against the Red Sox (all those lefty starters) or even the Yankees (Max Fried and Carlos Rodon) than the Rays or Guardians.

Toronto Blue Jays

Fatal flaw: Offense (29th in runs)

Vladimir Guerrero Jr.'s issues this season have been well documented -- just nine home runs, including only one at home -- but producing runs has been a teamwide issue, as nearly every player has seen his numbers drop from 2025. Like last season, the Jays are a high-contact lineup (only the Rays strike out less often), but even Kazuma Okamoto's 33 home runs haven't been enough to lift this group from the bottom of the majors in offense. Only the Angels have scored fewer runs. Maybe Guerrero turns it on if the Jays sneak in, but the lineup has shown no signs of making a deep October run.

stories.headline: Fantasy hockey rankings: Nathan MacKinnon, Connor McDavid lead 2026 rankings
stories.summary: After a busy NHL offseason, get ready for the 2026-27 fantasy hockey season with the top 250 rankings.
stories.body:
We've had a few weeks to digest the Brandon Bussi and the Carolina Hurricanes raising the Stanley Cup over their heads, Gavin McKenna going first overall in the 2026 NHL Draft, and seeing many of the league's best change teams this offseason. Now, the NHL has released the schedule for the 2026-27 season, so you can get excited about the best matchups and the lineup strategy for the 84-game regular season. Now it's time to think about what comes next, like where every player fits into your fantasy hockey strategy.

The top of the rankings should look familiar from where we left off, with Nathan MacKinnon, Connor McDavid and Hart Trophy-winner Nikita Kucherov leading the pack. Norris Trophy-winner Zach Werenski leads all defenseman and Tampa Bay Lightning goalie Andrei Vasilevskiy is the top-ranked goalie.

These rankings are based on the ESPN Fantasy standard game (for skaters: goals = 2 points, assists = 1 point, shots and hits = 0.1 points, blocked shots and special-teams points = 0.5 points; for goaltenders: wins = 4 points, OT losses = 1 point, shutouts = 3 points, saves = 0.2 points, goals against = -2 points).

stories.headline: Messi, MLS' Garber appear to have heated exchange after Miami win
stories.summary: Lionel Messi pointed his finger at MLS commissioner Don Garber on multiple occasions while speaking with him after Inter Miami's game with Cruz Azul on Wednesday.
stories.body:
MIAMI -- Lionel Messi pointed his finger at MLS commissioner Don Garber on multiple occasions while speaking with him after Inter Miami's game with Cruz Azul on Wednesday.

Postgame video showed Messi pointing at Garber and speaking to him before walking away. He then appears later in the video pointing at him and talking to him again. Another video showed them pointing at each other as they spoke.

MLS declined comment on the matter. Inter Miami didn't immediately respond to a request for comment.

The exchange came after Inter Miami defeated Cruz Azul 2-0 to win the Campeones Cup. Messi scored the 100th goal of his Inter Miami career during the game.

This victory gave Inter Miami another trophy three years after Messi's arrival. Miami won the Leagues Cup in 2023, the Supporters' Shield in 2024 and MLS Cup in 2025.

stories.headline: Alexa Grasso shows off flyweight's elite status in women's P4P top 10
stories.summary: Former UFC champion puts elite status of women's flyweight division on display in ESPN's P4P top 10.
stories.body:
It's uncommon for two fighters ranked in the pound-for-pound top 10 to meet in a bout with no championship at stake. But that was the case at Saturday's fourth annual Noche UFC, where Alexa Grasso faced Manon Fiorot.

Grasso is a former women's flyweight champion and Fiorot competed for the belt last year, so their status as MMA elites was well established before they fought. And when Grasso won by unanimous decision, she further solidified her standing in the ESPN women's pound-for-pound rankings.

The top five of the rankings remains intact, and Grasso moves up from 10th to replace Fiorot at No. 6. Fiorot slips two positions to No. 8 in a pound-for-pound hierarchy in which seven of the 10 ranked women compete at flyweight (including Zhang Weili, the former UFC strawweight champion who last fought in an unsuccessful challenge of Valentina Shevchenko in November).

With Shevchenko injured and having vacated her title, there will be much scrambling for the top spot, which will be at stake when No. 5 Natalia Silva fights unranked Wang Cong on Oct. 3.

For the ESPN divisional MMA rankings, click here.

Note: Results are current; rankings are as of Sept. 16. To be eligible for the rankings, a fighter must have competed over the past 12 months or must have an upcoming fight booked. Fighters who have been dropped for inactivity can be reinstated only after they compete.

Women's pound-for-pound rankings

1. Valentina Shevchenko

UFC flyweight

Record: 26-4-1

Last: W (UD) vs. Zhang Weili, Nov. 15, 2025

Next: TBA

Shevchenko's dominance came under question in 2022 and 2023, when she went 1-1-1 in a trilogy with Alexa Grasso. Boy, does that feel like a long time ago now. Shevchenko more than reasserted herself as the best flyweight in the world, and then she established herself as the No. 1 woman in the world, period. It wasn't surprising that she beat Zhang, but it was surprising how easy she made it look. Shevchenko is out injured, however, so she has vacated her UFC title, which will be up for grabs when Natalia Silva meets Wang Cong on Oct. 3.

2. Zhang Weili

UFC flyweight / strawweight

Record: 26-4

Last: L (UD) vs. Valentina Shevchenko, Nov. 15, 2025

Next: TBA

It's hard to move up in weight, especially at the highest level. That sounds like it should be obvious, but Zhang had been dominant at 115 pounds for so long, some of us might have taken for granted how big of a challenge moving to 125 would be. UFC 322 was a bad night for Zhang, but she doesn't have many. And if she decides to stay at flyweight, it certainly seems reasonable to believe she'll fare better in the future.

3. Cris Cyborg

PFL featherweight champion

Record: 30-2, 1 NC

Last: W (UD) vs. Ketlen Vieira, Aug. 22

Next: TBA

It had been a while since Cyborg had fought an elite opponent in MMA until she met Larissa Pacheco in 2024. That was a legitimate matchup -- and many within the industry were predicting Cyborg's downfall. Instead, she took out the PFL's two-weight champion, upending all of Pacheco's momentum. One of the original pioneers of women's MMA is once again a champion after getting her second career submission at PFL Lyon in December. The PFL promoted her fight with Vieira as a retirement bout, but after her win Cyborg did not sound like someone who is done fighting.

4. Mackenzie Dern

UFC strawweight champion

Record: 17-5

Last: W (UD) vs. Gillian Robertson, Aug. 15

Next: TBA

Dern's rise to the 115-pound throne was truly a changing of the guard. She is the division's first first-time champion since 2019, because the previous three champs -- Zhang Weili, Carla Esparza and Rose Namajunas -- all were in their second reigns. Dern, nearly a decade into her MMA career after multiple jiu-jitsu world championships, has won four fights in a row, including a dominant performance against a fellow grappling-heavy fighter, Robertson, in her first title defense.

5. Natalia Silva

UFC flyweight

Record: 20-5-1

Last: W (UD) vs. Rose Namajunas, Jan. 24

Next: Oct. 3 vs. Wang Cong

Silva is looking every bit the part of a future UFC champion following a dominant display against Alexa Grasso at UFC 315 and a victory over Namajunas at UFC 324. Silva's stick-and-move style has frustrated even the highest level of opponent, and she's got youth on her side as she won't turn 30 until 2027. With an injured Valentina Shevchenko having vacated the title, Silva will fight Wang for the belt at UFC 332.

6. Alexa Grasso

UFC flyweight

Previous ranking: 10

Record: 18-5-1

Last: W (UD) vs. Manon Fiorot, Sept. 12

Next: TBA

Grasso went nearly three years without winning a fight, but her 2023 win right before the skid was a huge one, a submission of Valentina Shevchenko for the UFC title. What followed were two more fights with Shevchenko -- a draw, then a loss -- and then a loss to Natalia Silva. But she reasserted herself with a finish of Maycee Barber in March, then got the best of Fiorot, a fellow title contender, at Noche UFC to put herself in position for another title shot.

7. Dakota Ditcheva

PFL flyweight

Record: 16-0

Last: W (UD) vs. Denise Kielholtz, July 31

Next: TBA

Not only did Ditcheva win the PFL's flyweight season in 2024, but she did so in spectacular fashion -- a TKO finish over Taila Santos, who once challenged for a UFC title. Ditcheva fought only once in 2025, dominating Sumiko Inaba in the co-main event of the first PFL Champions Series card in Cape Town, South Africa. She then spent over a year on the sideline, healing injuries to both hands, before returning at PFL New York with a dominant win over Kielholtz.

8. Manon Fiorot

UFC flyweight

Previous ranking: 6

Record: 13-3

Last: L (UD) vs. Alexa Grasso, Sept. 12

Next: TBA

Fiorot had handled everyone the UFC put in front of her -- except the champion, Valentina Shevchenko, who defeated the Frenchwoman at UFC 315 in May 2025. But then, with another title shot within her grasp, Fiorot ran into Grasso, a former champion, at Noche UFC and lost a competitive fight.

9. Erin Blanchfield

UFC flyweight

Previous ranking: 8

Record: 14-2

Last: W (Sub2) vs. Tracy Cortez, Nov. 15, 2025

Next: Oct. 17 vs. Jasmine Jasudavicius

Her rise toward the top of the division was derailed by a March 2024 loss to Manon Fiorot, but Blanchfield bounced back with two straight wins, including one over two-time former strawweight champion Rose Namajunas in November 2024. If she wins her October bout with Jasudavicius, a fellow top-10 flyweight contender, Blanchfield would inch ever closer to a title shot.

10. Tatiana Suarez

UFC strawweight

Previous ranking: 9

Record: 12-1

Last: W (Sub2) vs. Loopy Godínez, April 11

Next: TBA

If Suarez is still feeling the effects of last year's humbling defeat to Zhang Weili in a title challenge, she certainly didn't show it at UFC 327, overcoming early adversity to thrash Godinez, a fellow top-10 strawweight. Suarez is going to be a tough out for anyone at 115 pounds.

How our panel voted
Brett Okamoto: 1. Valentina Shevchenko; 2. Zhang Weili; 3. Mackenzie Dern; 4. Cris Cyborg; 5. Alexa Grasso; 6. Manon Fiorot; 7. Dakota Ditcheva; 8. Natalia Silva; 9. Erin Blanchfield; 10. Tatiana Suarez.

Carlos Contreras Legaspi: 1. Shevchenko; 2. Cyborg; 3. Zhang; 4. Dern; 5. Silva; 6. Grasso; 7. Ditcheva; 8. Suarez; 9. Fiorot; 10. Blanchfield.

Andrew Davis: 1. Shevchenko; 2. Zhang; 3. Cyborg; 4. Dern; 5. Silva; 6. Grasso; 7. Blanchfield; 8. Ditcheva; 9. Suarez; 10. Fiorot.

Dre Waters: 1. Shevchenko; 2. Zhang; 3. Cyborg; 4. Silva; 5. Dern; 6. Grasso; 7. Ditcheva; 8. Blanchfield; 9. Fiorot; 10. Suarez.

Jeff Wagenheim: 1. Shevchenko; 2. Zhang; 3. Cyborg; 4. Silva; 5. Grasso; 6. Dern; 7. Fiorot; 8. Blanchfield; 9. Suarez; 10. Ditcheva.

Men's pound-for-pound rankings

1. Islam Makhachev

UFC welterweight champion

Record: 29-1

Last: W (UD) vs. Ian Machado Garry, Aug. 15

Next: TBA

Makhachev vacated the UFC lightweight championship to go for a second title at welterweight. By winning that belt last November with a thrashing of Jack Della Maddalena, Makhachev staked his place among MMA's greatest -- not just in today's sport but of all time. His win over Machado Garry at UFC 330 was his 17th straight, breaking the UFC record for consecutive wins. Makhachev is piling up unprecedented achievements.

2. Petr Yan

UFC bantamweight champion

Record: 20-5

Last: W (UD) vs. Merab Dvalishvili, Dec. 6, 2025

Next: Oct. 24 vs. Dvalishvili

What a return to the top it's been for Yan. He began his career with 15 consecutive wins before going on a 1-4 run from 2021 to 2023. That almost doesn't feel real now, after watching him reclaim his throne against Dvalishvili, who once handed him the worst loss of his career. Yan took a major detour, but this was the destination we felt he was capable of before the skid. He once again looks like one of the best fighters on the planet. He can prove it by beating Dvalishvili again.

3. Merab Dvalishvili

UFC bantamweight

Record: 21-5

Last: L (UD) vs. Petr Yan, Dec. 6, 2025

Next: Oct. 24 vs. Yan

Dvalishvili was on one of the most impressive runs through the UFC's bantamweight division ever. Not only did he defeat Sean O'Malley for the second time in nine months at UFC 316, but he showcased a new part of his game, finishing O'Malley with a guillotine. Starting in August 2022, Dvalishvili beat José Aldo, Yan, Henry Cejudo, O'Malley (twice), Umar Nurmagomedov and Cory Sandhagen. But at UFC 323, in an attempt to become the first champion in UFC history to successfully defend a title four times in a calendar year, Dvalishvili lost a rematch with Yan. They will fight for a third time at UFC 333.

4. Tom Aspinall

UFC heavyweight

Record: 15-3, 1 NC

Last: NC1 vs. Ciryl Gane, Oct. 25, 2025

Next: TBA

You can make a case that Aspinall is the most dynamic, skillful, talented heavyweight the sport has seen. He is dominating opponents in a way that is unmatched. No one can last a round with him. He had hoped to prove his supremacy against Jon Jones, but Jones opted to retire, elevating Aspinall from interim champion. His first defense of the undisputed belt ended anticlimactically, as an eye poke resulted in his UFC 321 fight with Gane being declared a no-contest. Still recovering from the eye injury, Aspinall vacated his title on Sept. 14.

5. Ilia Topuria

UFC lightweight

Record: 17-1

Last: L (TKO4) vs. Justin Gaethje, June 14

Next: TBA

Topuria was an undefeated two-division champion when he ran into Gaethje at UFC Freedom 250 and was brutalized in a stoppage loss. How will that affect the immediate future of Topuria? His knockout wins over two of the greatest featherweights, Alexander Volkanovski and Max Holloway, gave him an intimidating aura. Can the former champion get that back?

6. Justin Gaethje

UFC lightweight champion

Record: 28-5

Last: W (TKO4) vs. Ilia Topuria, June 14

Next: TBA

Gaethje has spent his 15-year career thrilling MMA fans, but before the title bout on the White House lawn, all he had to show for it -- aside from 15 bonus checks in 15 UFC appearances -- were two missed opportunities to be an undisputed champion. His fourth-round TKO of Topuria got Gaethje over the hump. It was a resilient performance in a back-and-forth battle that is a prime candidate for fight of the year. More important for Gaethje: At age 37, he is finally sitting at the top of the mountain.

7. Alexander Volkanovski

UFC featherweight champion

Record: 28-4

Last: W (UD) vs. Diego Lopes, Jan. 31

Next: Oct. 24 vs. Movsar Evloev

It felt as if the sport had started to write Volkanovski's eulogy following his knockout loss to Ilia Topuria in February 2024. Volkanovski noticed and made a point of proving to everyone he still has plenty left by recapturing the featherweight belt at UFC 314, the first of two consecutive wins over Lopes. His age (37) will likely continue to be a prefight topic, which is fine because Volkanovski enjoys proving people wrong. Can he hand Evloev his first loss at UFC 333?

8. Alexandre Pantoja

UFC flyweight

Record: 30-6

Last: L (TKO1) vs. Joshua Van, Dec. 6, 2025

Next: Sept. 19 vs. Joshua Van

Pantoja became the UFC's unquestioned flyweight king by racking up four title defenses, including two in pay-per-view main events in 2024. He built his winning streak to eight in his UFC 317 win over Kai Kara-France, whom he had already defeated before, like other challengers. But he lost his belt in a gruesome way, injuring his elbow in the opening seconds of a UFC 323 fight with Van. Pantoja gets his rematch with Van at UFC 331.

9. Ciryl Gane

UFC heavyweight interim champion

Record: 14-2, 1 NC

Last: W (TKO2) vs. Alex Pereira, June 14

Next: TBA

Gane is unique in that he is the first -- and could very well go down as the only -- heavyweight to face the division's four biggest names in Francis Ngannou, Jon Jones, Tom Aspinall and Pereira. None of those four have fought each other, yet all four have have fought the Frenchman. Gane was 0-2 with a no-contest against that group before he knocked out Pereira in the second round of their interim title fight. Gane was heralded as the future of the generation when he broke onto the scene, but endured growing pains in losses to Ngannou and Jones. He looks formidable now, and no one will be counting him out if he faces Aspinall in a title unification bout.

10. Alex Pereira

UFC heavyweight / light heavyweight

Record: 13-4

Last: L (TKO2) vs. Ciryl Gane, June 14

Next: TBA

He was on the verge of making history when the opportunity fell apart. Pereira was a UFC champion at middleweight, then light heavyweight, but his unprecedented pursuit of a belt in a third weight class did not go well for the Brazilian, who lost an interim heavyweight title fight to Gane on the White House card. At 39 years old, Pereira does not have much time left to recapture the magic.

Other fighters receiving votes: Joshua Van and Arman Tsarukyan.

stories.headline: I raced against Max Verstappen ... for 10 seconds: Inside the chaos of Max vs 100
stories.summary: ESPN's Nate Saunders might not have lasted long in Max vs 100, but it was still a memorable event. Here, he reflects on his karting experience with Formula 1's Max Verstappen
stories.body:
Few can say they have raced against Max Verstappen -- even if they can only boast that they stayed in front of him for all of 10 seconds.

That was about as long as my challenge lasted in Max vs 100, a wonderfully simple concept on Disney+: put four-time world champion Verstappen at the back of a 101-kart grid at Silverstone and give him 30 laps to pass everybody in front of him. Once he passed you, your race was over.

Starting 89th, I was eliminated before my kart had even reached the front of the grid we were all racing from.

A humbling experience, no doubt: but should an amateur karter going up against one of the greatest drivers of all time have expected any different?

It wasn't just me who had a blink-and-you-missed-it moment against Verstappen. He dispatched an astonishing 64 drivers in that first lap alone and needed only 13 more to catch and overtake everyone else.

Verstappen enjoyed it so much he teased doing it again next year against 200. Seeing how quickly he got things done on Wednesday, you would not bet against him completing that challenge with a handful of laps to spare, either.

Starting as low as I did, there was probably not much chance of any other outcome for me. I already had the excuses ready to explain my lowly grid slot. A spin during one-shot qualifying had turned what was already a middling-to-below-average lap into one only good enough to occupy the 45th row of the grid. Shoot. A blow, I told myself, of getting down to Turn 1 in one piece and an even bigger blow for my chances of staying ahead of Verstappen for even a few corners. Perhaps a better lap and grid position would have given me a better buffer to prevent the inevitable, I reasoned, while Verstappen struggled to get past the slower karts in the field.

- Max vs 100: Verstappen jokes taking on '200' drivers next time

- Max Verstappen wins Max vs 100 in style after overtaking 100 go-karters

Turns out the excuses weren't necessary -- an improved grid spot wouldn't have made a shred of difference. As the red lights at the beginning of the start procedure went on one by one, Verstappen had rocked his kart backwards and forwards in a bouncing motion, an old trick he said he learned racing as a seven-year-old. It meant his kart was already rolling well enough to breeze past the karts nearest to him as the lights turned green.

I knew no such tricks, so like the majority of the other amateurs, moved off the line sluggishly as I set about looked for a racing line through the blur of cars down towards Turn 1.

Approximately 10 seconds later, as some space opened up around me as I came off the curve and onto the straight, I glanced to my right.

There he was.

And then, he wasn't.

Verstappen breezed on by as though he was driving a different category of vehicle altogether. As that part of the field got to the first corner, karts were spinning left and right, but he threaded through the chaos like a slalom skier, at one stage simply taking to the grass when the conventional route vanished. My own kart got turned around -- perhaps because I was as much watching the disappearing Verstappen as I was the disappearing bit of unoccupied tarmac in front of me. It is easy to forget when watching trackside or TV the remarkable control of a vehicle professionals had -- Verstappen seemed to be racing on rails, even when he was driving off track to pass karts facing the wrong way.

So that was it. 10 seconds after racing Verstappen had started, my race against Verstappen was over. Brutal stuff indeed.

It all happened so fast that some of the 64 who slowly trundled back into the pit lane after elimination were not even convinced they had seen Verstappen go by. By the time I was out of the kart, he was up to 20th.

"I think the first lap went a bit better than expected, so that helps a lot," Verstappen said later.

Organisers had set a limit of 30 laps but that seemed ludicrously generous as he scythed his way through the field. There had been talk beforehand about trying to defend, working together or even making Verstappen fight for each position. When asked about advice for the 100 karters ahead of the event, Verstappen's long-time rival George Russell had joked that participants should try and go four or five-wide and effectively block the road to stop him advancing. There was, of course, not even the slightest bit of coordination between anyone at the back of the field once the lights went out. Even if we had, Verstappen appeared more than happy to take to the grass on a couple of occasions to get to where he needed to be.

"You just act on instinct, whatever happens when the lights go out, you kind of just see where the gaps are and then you also kind of need to trust the few people around you that they don't do anything crazy," Verstappen said later. "But to be honest, they didn't."

Even if no-one was driving like crazy, the chaos at the start was predictable. Race director and circuit designer David Terrien -- who raced against Max's parents Jos Verstappen and Sophie Kumpen when they were junior karters -- later said he doubted there has ever been a kart race featuring 101 karts. That's not surprising, as there did not seem to be quite enough road to accommodate everyone at the beginning. The grid stretched down the main straight and around a curve. The first lap was almost immediately put under caution -- there were spins, mine included, at Turn 1, while two karts crashed at Turn 3 further up the track so badly that a group of 10 karts got stuck behind.

The circuit worked well when the field had been trimmed down, though, with Verstappen's progress slowing as the amateurs on track were wittled down. He spent six laps in fourth, slowly reeling in the runaway trio at the front.

Verstappen ended up beating one journalist who did, at least, manage to do a better job of representing for the F1 paddock: Dutch reporter Jacky Martens, who finished ahead of YouTuber Zac Alsop and Red Bull's own Lewis Osler to be crowned best of the amateurs. Those last laps were entertaining to watch on the stream, as Verstappen got to utilise the microphones he had fitted to his balaclava to talk to the other competitors around him. "I'm coming for you," he said to a contestant at one stage. Later, he told commentators Alex Jacques and Matt Gallagher: "They need to focus because I'm definitely catching them."

Several of those who remained at least got to properly experience what racing Verstappen is all about. Late in the contest, one of the racers joked to Verstappen -- via a microphone which linked the Dutchman to drivers he approached -- that all he could hear in his head was the famous song about him: "Duh Duh Duh Duh, Max Verstappen, Duh Duh Duh Duh."

Another turned to Verstappen as he approached, laughing and putting his hands together as if begging him not to overtake. He's not the only one to have felt like this with the Dutchman approaching him at alarming speed. McLaren CEO Zak Brown joked last year, as Verstappen started reeling in McLaren pair Lando Norris and Oscar Piastri in the championship, that Verstappen was like the T-Rex in Jurassic Park, seen chasing the car in the mirror with the warning 'Objects in the mirror are closer than they appear.' My experience of being passed by Verstappen was so quick I didn't even get the chance to experience the fear.

For Verstappen, it seemed like enormous fun -- he later said he had not driven a proper go-kart since 2016. In a year which has seen Verstappen's love of Formula 1 tested on a massive scale, he later joked he would cherish his winners' trophy as it was his first of the year so far.

Verstappen recently signed a contract to stay in Formula 1 with Red Bull into 2030, ending several years of speculation about moves elsewhere. It's perhaps not surprising he can't imagine a future away from the company which first brought him into Formula 1 as a 17-year-old in 2015. "It's just great that with Red Bull they always come up with some crazy fun things and it suits me as well," he said. "I can really be myself and I think also the way it was organised today, I know that it requires a lot of effort to be able to do something like this."

Whether I'll be there on the grid with him for a future event remains to be seen -- if Wednesday's contest had been an audition to race against a Formula 1 legend again, I dismally failed.

But, given how Verstappen did make almost 100 people look like complete amateurs, there doesn't seem to be too much shame in that.

stories.headline: Borussia Dortmund teenager Konstantinos Karetsas returns to training after Champions League health scare
stories.summary: Borussia Dortmund says 18-year-old midfielder Konstantinos Karetsas is back in training just over a week after he slumped to the ground in an alarming medical incident on his Champions League debut.
stories.body:
Borussia Dortmund have said 18-year-old midfielder Konstantinos Karetsas is back in training just over a week after he slumped to the ground in an alarming medical incident on his Champions League debut.

Karetsas passed the ball to a teammate then signaled his distress to the referee before sitting on the grass during Dortmund's 3-2 win over Villarreal on Sept. 8.

He was in tears as he was stretchered off with suspected circulatory problems and was then taken to a hospital, where he stayed for much of last week.

"Konstantinos Karetsas is back in team training as of Wednesday after doing individual sessions at the start of the week," Dortmund said. "It was his first joint session with his teammates after he was taken off with circulatory problems in the game against Villarreal."

Dortmund hasn't specified the nature of any diagnosis for Karetsas, who was signed from Genk for a reported fee of $34.6 million last month, and didn't indicate whether he would be able to play Saturday against Stuttgart in the Bundesliga.

Karetsas plays internationally for Greece but was born in Belgium, where local media have reported that dehydration was suspected as a factor.

"I'm doing really well," he said in a video recorded during a visit to his old club Genk and published Monday on X. "We tested everything and everything is fine. I just need to adjust a bit to the intensity but that will come with time."

"I went out with him but in that moment, he wasn't able to speak," Book said.

- Borussia Dortmund teenager Karetsas hospitalised after slumping to turf in Champions League

Karetsas was able to cheer on his teammates from the stands in Saturday's 3-0 win over Paderborn.

Managing director Lars Ricken said there had been "no warning signs" of any circulatory problems prior to the incident.

stories.headline: 'It's all on': Fitzgibbon relishes Robbo coaching duel
stories.summary: Mates and mentors Craig Fitzgibbon and Trent Robinson have banned contact this week as the Cronulla and Sydney Roosters coaches chase an NRL preliminary final.
stories.body:
No more Mr Nice Guy, Craig Fitzgibbon has shoved friendship aside as he plots to shatter the Sydney Roosters' NRL title hopes for a second successive season.

After a decorated playing career with the Roosters, highlighted by his Clive Churchill-winning display in the Tricolours' 2002 premiership triumph, Fitzgibbon enjoyed a fruitful decade working under Trent Robinson as the club's assistant coach.

But that friendly relationship is on ice this week, with Fitzgibbon, wearing his Cronulla coaching hat, intent on ending the Roosters' season as the Sharks did last year with a 20-10 first-week ambush.

"It was a long time. I've had 10 years working with Trent, so it's definitely a long apprenticeship," Fitzgibbon said ahead of Saturday night's do-or-die battle at Allianz Stadium.

"I had plenty of lessons and am forever grateful for my time there and his mentoring of me to be a coach.

"And he was always supportive and backed me in to take the opportunity when that comes, so I'll be forever grateful for that.

"But this week is about Sharks versus Roosters and, whilst we talk regularly, we're not talking this week."

The latest episode in the pair's coaching rivalry will be the third time in the past four seasons that Cronulla and the Roosters clash in a sudden-death final, with Fitzgibbon and Robinson splitting the first two September showdowns.

The Roosters edged the Sharks 13-12 in 2023 before last year's loss.

Texting is taboo this week, with Fitzgibbon happy to wait until after fulltime to rekindle their great mateship.

"He's fine with that too," Fitzgibbon said.

"He's just as competitive as I am so, no, we'll shut it down this week. We've bumped into each other in plenty of semis now, so it's a contest and it's a game.

"A lot of work goes into a whole season, starting all the way back in the November before, so the ups and downs of the season.

"But you get to this end and it's all on."

Both sides fumbled and bumbled their way into this year's finals, the Sharks losing four of their last five regular-season games with star five-eighth Braydon Trindall sidelined with a dislocated shoulder.

After briefly sharing premiership favouritism after taking down Penrith in round 24, the Roosters also lost playmaker Sam Walker to an ankle injury during a run of four straight defeats.

While below the form that led the Sharks to nine wins from 10 starts before their slump, Fitzgibbon saw enough in last Saturday's 26-16 victory over North Queensland to be heartened.

"We played more like Sharks," he said.

"A bit more cohesion back in. Obviously there were some changes in and out and then we set on the line-up and got back to playing like we know we can.

"It was probably really physical early and we had to stay in the fight there for a bit and then managed to come out the other side and dealt with a couple of disallowed tries and dealt with a little bit of adversity to be able to not get flustered and stick to the plan."

Saturday night's victors will advance to a preliminary final against the Dolphins at Suncorp Stadium next Friday night.
